content: The FCAR gene in humans encodes the transmembrane receptor FcαRI, also known as CD89 (Cluster of Differentiation 89). This receptor specifically binds to the heavy-chain constant region of Immunoglobulin A (IgA) antibodies. FcαRI is expressed on the surface of myeloid lineage cells, such as neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, and eosinophils. However, it is notably absent from intestinal macrophages and mast cells. The receptor plays a dual role in immune responses, mediating both pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory effects depending on the state of the IgA molecule bound to it. FcαRI requires a process called inside-out signaling to be primed for ligand binding. This priming is initiated by cytokines signaling the presence of an infection, which activate the kinase PI3K. PI3K subsequently activates p38 and PKC, which, along with PP2A, lead to the dephosphorylation of the serine 263 residue (Ser263) on the intracellular domain of the FcαRI α-chain. This priming process does not depend on the association of FcαRI with the Fc receptor γ-chain (FcR γ-chain) but does require cytoskeletal organization. Once primed, FcαRI can bind IgA, with its extracellular domain EC1 interacting with the hinge region between the IgA-Fc regions Ca2 and Ca3. The FcαRI α-chain consists of two extracellular domains (EC1 and EC2) arranged at a right angle to each other, a transmembrane domain, and an intracellular domain. However, the α-chain alone cannot signal in response to IgA binding. FcαRI must associate with a dimeric form of the FcR γ-chain, which contains immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) at its ends. The FcR γ-chain is responsible for transmitting the signal into the cell. Two alleles of FCAR, differing by a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP), encode FcαRI molecules with distinct abilities to signal for the production and release of IL-6 and TNF-α. This SNP results in either serine or glycine at the 248th residue of the amino acid sequence, located in the intracellular domain of FcαRI. Compared to FcαRI with Ser248, FcαRI molecules with Gly248 are more effective at signaling for IL-6 release, even independently of FcR γ-chain association. Alternative splicing of the FCAR gene transcript produces ten mRNA variants encoding different isoforms. The signaling and cellular responses mediated by FcαRI depend on the state of the IgA molecules bound to it. When IgA molecules in immune complexes bind to multiple FcαRI receptors, a pro-inflammatory response is triggered. This involves the activation of Src family kinases and the phosphorylation of FcR γ-chain ITAMs by Lyn. The tyrosine kinase Syk then docks at the phosphorylated ITAMs and initiates PI3K and PLC-γ signaling cascades. These cascades lead to pro-inflammatory responses, including cytokine release, phagocytosis, respiratory bursts, antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity, production of reactive oxygen species, and antigen presentation. Despite ITAM signaling typically initiating activation cascades, FcαRI can act as either an activating or inhibitory receptor. Inhibitory ITAM signaling (ITAMi) results in anti-inflammatory responses. When FcαRI monovalently binds monomeric, non-antigen-bound IgA (the most common form in serum), the resulting signals inactivate other activating receptors, such as FcγR and FcεRI. This occurs because Lyn only partially phosphorylates the FcR γ-chain ITAMs, leading to the recruitment of SHP-1 (Src homology region 2 domain-containing phosphatase-1), a tyrosine phosphatase. SHP-1 coordinates the anti-inflammatory response by preventing other receptors from becoming phosphorylated and signaling for pro-inflammatory responses. This ITAMi signaling supports homeostasis in the absence of pathogens. The anti-inflammatory role of monomeric IgA-FcαRI binding has potential therapeutic implications for allergic asthma. Targeting FcαRI in transgenic mouse models with anti-FcαRI Fab antibodies, which mimic the binding of monomeric IgA, resulted in decreased infiltration of airway tissue by inflammatory leukocytes. The secreted form of IgA (sIgA), a homodimer secreted across epithelial linings such as the gut epithelium, is sterically hindered in its binding to FcαRI. This is due to a section of the cleaved polymeric Ig receptor that obscures some of sIgA’s FcαRI binding site. However, the precursor to sIgA, dimeric IgA (dIgA), binds to FcαRI with approximately the same affinity as monomeric IgA. Secreted IgA plays a critical role in preventing immune responses to commensal gut microbes, which is why intestinal macrophages do not express FcαRI. During mucosal tissue invasion by pathogenic bacteria, neutrophils responding to the infection bind and phagocytose dIgA-opsonized bacteria via FcαRI. FcαRI is also an important Fc receptor for neutrophil-mediated killing of tumor cells. When FcαRI-expressing neutrophils encounter IgA-opsonized tumor cells, they not only perform antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity but also release the cytokines TNF-α and IL-1β, which enhance neutrophil migration to the site. FcαRI interacts with FcγR1A, as demonstrated in studies.
